claim: Bacterial exonuclease III (ExoIII) has been documented as a DNA repair-associated nuclease with apurinic/apyrimidinic (AP)-endonuclease and 3′→5′ exonuclease activities.
source: Bacterial exonuclease III (ExoIII), widely acknowledged for specifically targeting double-stranded DNA (dsDNA), has been documented as a DNA repair-associated nuclease with apurinic/apyrimidinic (AP)-endonuclease and 3′→5′ exonuclease activities.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature on ExoIII's known enzymatic activities.

claim: ExoIII has been broadly applied in molecular biosensors due to its enzymatic properties.
source: Due to these enzymatic properties, ExoIII has been broadly applied in molecular biosensors.
evidence: This claim is supported by references to the application of ExoIII in biosensors based on its known enzymatic properties.

claim: ExoIII (Escherichia coli) possesses highly active enzymatic activities on ssDNA.
source: Here, we demonstrate that ExoIII (Escherichia coli) possesses highly active enzymatic activities on ssDNA.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data using fluorescence-quenching reporters and mass spectrometry analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: ExoIII cleaved ssDNA at the 5′-bond of phosphodiester from 3′ to 5′ end by both exonuclease and endonuclease activities.
source: By using a range of ssDNA fluorescence-quenching reporters and fluorophore-labeled probes coupled with mass spectrometry analysis, we found ExoIII cleaved the ssDNA at 5′-bond of phosphodiester from 3′ to 5′ end by both exonuclease and endonuclease activities.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from fluorescence-quenching assays and mass spectrometry analysis.

claim: Point mutation analysis identified critical residues for the ssDNase action of ExoIII.
source: Additional point mutation analysis identified the critical residues for the ssDNase action of ExoIII and suggested the activity shared the same active center with the dsDNA-targeted activities of ExoIII.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from point mutation studies.

claim: The ssDNase activity of ExoIII shares the same active center with the dsDNA-targeted activities of ExoIII.
source: Additional point mutation analysis identified the critical residues for the ssDNase action of ExoIII and suggested the activity shared the same active center with the dsDNA-targeted activities of ExoIII.
evidence: This claim is supported by inference from point mutation analysis data.

claim: ExoIII can digest dsDNA structures containing 3′-end ssDNA.
source: Notably, ExoIII could also digest the dsDNA structures containing 3′-end ssDNA.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data on various dsDNA substrates.

claim: Most ExoIII-assisted molecular biosensors require the involvement of single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) or nucleic acid aptamer containing ssDNA.
source: Considering most ExoIII-assisted molecular biosensors require the involvement of single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) or nucleic acid aptamer containing ssDNA, the activity will lead to low efficiency or false positive outcome.
evidence: This claim is supported by knowledge of ExoIII-based biosensor design and citations to relevant literature.

claim: The ssDNase activity of ExoIII will lead to low efficiency or false positive outcomes in ExoIII-assisted molecular biosensors.
source: Considering most ExoIII-assisted molecular biosensors require the involvement of single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) or nucleic acid aptamer containing ssDNA, the activity will lead to low efficiency or false positive outcome.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the demonstrated ssDNase activity and its implications for biosensor performance.

claim: Base damage is one of the most common DNA lesions caused by alkylation, oxidation, deamination, and depurination/depyrimidination.
source: Base damage is one of the most common DNA lesions caused by alkylation, oxidation, deamination, and depurination/depyrimidination (Robertson et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Robertson et al., 2009.

claim: ExoIII has been widely recognized as one of the most critical players in base excision repair (BER).
source: ExoIII has been widely recognized as one of the most critical players in BER (Lovett, 2011; Lee et al., 2022; Mol et al., 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Lovett, 2011; Lee et al., 2022; Mol et al., 1995.

claim: BER has been conceptually divided into five steps: glycosylase excision, AP endonuclease incision, 5′-deoxyribose phosphate removal, polymerase-directed gap filling, and ligase-aided nick sealing.
source: Based on the enzymatic activities involved, BER has been conceptually divided into the following five steps (Centore et al., 2008): (1) glycosylase excision on the damaged base forming the apurinic/apyrimidinic (AP) site; (2) AP endonuclease (ExoIII) incision on the phosphodiester backbone to create and extend a ssDNA gap; (3) 5′-deoxyribose phosphate (dRp) removal; (4) polymerase-directed gap filling; (5) ligase-aided nick sealing.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Centore et al., 2008.

claim: ExoIII performs dual roles of AP endonuclease and exonuclease in E. coli during the BER process.
source: During the BER process, ExoIII performs the dual roles of AP endonuclease and exonuclease in E. coli (Rogers and Weiss, 1980).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Rogers and Weiss, 1980.

claim: ExoIII first acts as an endonuclease to hydrolyze the phosphodiester bond at the 5′-end of the AP site, then as an exonuclease to degrade the downstream single-stranded DNA of the duplex region from 3′ to 5′ end.
source: Once the damaged bases are removed by glycosylases leaving an AP site, ExoIII first acts as an endonuclease to hydrolyze the phosphodiester bond at the 5′-end of the AP site, then as an exonuclease to degrade the downstream single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) of the duplex region from 3′ to 5′ end.
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge of ExoIII function in BER.

claim: The two ExoIII-dominated enzymatic activities create a proper length of ssDNA gap on dsDNA, which is required for polymerase binding at the locus to re-synthesize nucleotides.
source: These two ExoIII-dominated enzymatic activities create a proper length of ssDNA gap on dsDNA, which is required for polymerase binding at the locus to re-synthesize nucleotides (Yoo et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Yoo et al., 2021.

claim: The αM helix of ExoIII stabilized the substrate by stretching into the major groove of dsDNA in the catalytic process.
source: Structural analysis revealed that the αM helix of ExoIII stabilized the substrate by stretching into the major groove of dsDNA in the catalytic process Mol et al., 1995.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Mol et al., 1995 and structural analysis.

claim: The multiple activities of ExoIII on dsDNA lie in the same active site.
source: Interestingly, different from the typical multifunctional enzymes, i.e., DNA polymerase (Biertümpfel et al., 2010), with separate active sites, the multiple activities of ExoIII on dsDNA lie in the same active site (Lee et al., 2022; Mol et al., 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Lee et al., 2022; Mol et al., 1995.

claim: During the 1960s-1990s, Kornberg's laboratory demonstrated that ExoIII specifically recognizes dsDNA but is inactive to ssDNA based on an ssDNA oligo of five consecutive Ts.
source: During the 1960s-1990s, Kornberg's laboratory demonstrated that ExoIII specifically recognizes dsDNA but is inactive to ssDNA based on an ssDNA oligo of five consecutive Ts (5′ pTpTpTpTpT 3′) (Richardson and Kornberg, 1964; Richardson et al., 1964), and other researchers showed ExoIII had limited enzymatic activity on dsDNA containing 3′-protruding ssDNA (≥4 nt) (Henikoff, 1984; Hoheisel, 1993).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Richardson and Kornberg, 1964; Richardson et al., 1964.

claim: Other researchers showed ExoIII had limited enzymatic activity on dsDNA containing 3′-protruding ssDNA (≥4 nt).
source: During the 1960s-1990s, Kornberg's laboratory demonstrated that ExoIII specifically recognizes dsDNA but is inactive to ssDNA based on an ssDNA oligo of five consecutive Ts (5′ pTpTpTpTpT 3′) (Richardson and Kornberg, 1964; Richardson et al., 1964), and other researchers showed ExoIII had limited enzymatic activity on dsDNA containing 3′-protruding ssDNA (≥4 nt) (Henikoff, 1984; Hoheisel, 1993).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Henikoff, 1984; Hoheisel, 1993.

claim: ExoIII was previously proposed to produce ssDNA from dsDNA.
source: Hence, ExoIII was previously proposed to produce ssDNA from dsDNA (Smith, 1979).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Smith, 1979.

claim: ExoIII has been widely employed in detecting nucleic acids, metals, toxins, and other types of small molecules when combined with novel materials, chemicals, or mechanical platforms.
source: Combined with novel materials, chemicals, or mechanical platforms, ExoIII has been widely employed in detecting nucleic acids, metals, toxins, and other types of small molecules (Liu et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Liu et al., 2021.

claim: ExoIII-assisted biosensors can be divided into two categories: AP-endonuclease and exonuclease-based methods.
source: Based on the specific enzymatic activities of ExoIII on dsDNA in detections, the ExoIII-assisted biosensors can be divided into two categories: AP-endonuclease and exonuclease-based methods.
evidence: This claim is based on knowledge of ExoIII-based biosensor design.

claim: TwistAmp Liquid exo kit represents one of the most successful AP-endonuclease-based nucleic acid detection as a promising replacement for PCR technique.
source: As a promising replacement for PCR technique (Stringer et al., 2018), TwistAmp Liquid exo kit (https://www.twistdx.co.uk/product/twistamp-liquid-exo/) represents one of the most successful AP-endonuclease-based nucleic acid detection, which combines recombinase polymerase amplification (RPA) (Piepenburg et al., 2006) and ExoIII.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Stringer et al., 2018 and Piepenburg et al., 2006.

claim: In the TwistAmp Liquid exo kit application, a 46~52 nt ssDNA probe is required to base-pair with the target sequence and should contain an AP site labeled with a fluorophore and a quencher.
source: In the application of the commercial kit, a 46~52 nt ssDNA probe is required to base-pair with the target sequence and the probe should also contain an AP site (usually simulated by a tetrahydrofuran [THF] residue) labeled with a fluorophore and a quencher, respectively, at or near the 5′- and 3′- end of AP.
evidence: This claim is based on knowledge of the TwistAmp Liquid exo kit design.

claim: Once the ssDNA probe binds to the complementary sequence with the aid of recombinase and forms a dsDNA region containing an AP, ExoIII recognizes and cleaves the AP site, which separates the fluorophore and quencher, leading to a fluorescence release.
source: Once the ssDNA probe binds to the complementary sequence with the aid of recombinase and forms a dsDNA region containing an AP, ExoIII recognizes and cleaves the AP site, which separates the fluorophore and quencher, leading to a fluorescence release.
evidence: This claim describes the mechanism of the TwistAmp Liquid exo kit based on established knowledge.

claim: In exonuclease-based methods, ssDNA or nucleic acid aptamer contained ssDNA is often configured to form dsDNA substrate for the exonuclease activity of ExoIII.
source: In the exonuclease-based methods, ssDNA or nucleic acid aptamer contained ssDNA is often configured to form dsDNA substrate for the exonuclease activity of ExoIII (Liu et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Liu et al., 2021.

claim: The digesting of ExoIII on ssDNA probe has been inadvertently observed in three ExoIII-developed detection methods and a biochemical study.
source: However, the digesting of ExoIII on ssDNA probe has been inadvertently observed in three ExoIII-developed detection methods (Cai et al., 2014; Xu et al., 2012; Shen et al., 2023) and a biochemical study (Yang et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Cai et al., 2014; Xu et al., 2012; Shen et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2007.

claim: ExoIII has still been publicly described, studied, and commercialized as a dsDNA-specific enzyme that is inactive or has limited activity on ssDNA for over a half-century.
source: ExoIII has, therefore, still been publicly described (https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/biochemistry-genetics-and-molecular-biology/exonuclease-III), studied (Lovett, 2011; Lee et al., 2022; Yoo et al., 2021; Shevelev and Hübscher, 2002), and commercialized as a dsDNA-specific enzyme that is inactive or has limited activity on ssDNA (https://www.thermofisher.cn/order/catalog/product/EN0191 and https://international.neb.com/products/m0206-exonuclease-iii-e-coli#Product%20Information) for over a half-century.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Lovett, 2011; Lee et al., 2022; Yoo et al., 2021; Shevelev and Hübscher, 2002 and references to commercial sources.

claim: The definition of the enzymatic activity of ExoIII on ssDNA remains ambiguous.
source: The definition of the enzymatic activity of ExoIII on ssDNA remains ambiguous.
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' assessment of the current state of knowledge.

claim: Fluorescence-quenching (FQ) is distance-dependent, where increasing the distance between the fluorophore and the quencher increases the fluorescence intensity.
source: FQ is distance-dependent, where increasing the distance between the fluorophore and the quencher increases the fluorescence intensity.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge of fluorescence-quenching principles.

claim: FQ has been transformed into one of the most influential techniques for monitoring dynamic alterations of macromolecule conformation in complex interactions.
source: As a sensitive and visible physical phenomenon, it has been transformed into one of the most influential techniques for monitoring dynamic alterations of macromolecule conformation in complex interactions (Mátyus et al., 2006; Zhuang et al., 2000; Kasry et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Mátyus et al., 2006; Zhuang et al., 2000; Kasry et al., 2012.

claim: The DNA or RNA-constructed FQ reporter has been successfully employed in CRISPR-based diagnostics as an efficient sensor of collateral trans-cleavage activity of Cas12a on ssDNA and Cas13a on RNA.
source: The DNA or RNA-constructed FQ reporter has been successfully employed in CRISPR-based diagnostics (Kaminski et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2024) as an efficient sensor of collateral trans-cleavage activity of Cas12a on ssDNA (Chen et al., 2018) and Cas13a on RNA (Gootenberg et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kaminski et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2018; Gootenberg et al., 2017.

claim: Once the nuclease cuts the ssDNA or RNA connector and disconnects the fluorophore and quencher, fluorescence will be significantly released as a positive readout for the detection.
source: Once the nuclease cuts the ssDNA or RNA connector and disconnects the fluorophore and quencher, fluorescence will be significantly released as a positive readout for the detection.
evidence: This claim describes the mechanism of FQ reporter-based detection based on established knowledge.

claim: ExoIII (5 U/µl) triggered a substantial fluorescent signal promptly upon adding to FQ reporter (5 µM) and most of the ssDNA substrate (over 90%) was cleaved in the first minute.
source: In contrast to T7 exo and LbCas12a, ExoIII (5 U/µl) triggered a substantial fluorescent signal promptly upon adding to FQ reporter (5 µM) (a total of 50 pmol), and most of the ssDNA substrate (over 90%) was cleaved in the first minute (Figure 1B), which suggested that the commercial ExoIII (5 U/µl) degraded over 2.7×1013 (45 pmol) phosphodiester bonds per minute in the reaction, significantly faster than 0.7 pmol phosphodiester bonds per minute of LbCas12a and that of other nucleases (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The commercial ExoIII (5 U/µl) degraded over 2.7×10^13 (45 pmol) phosphodiester bonds per minute in the reaction, significantly faster than 0.7 pmol phosphodiester bonds per minute of LbCas12a.
source: In contrast to T7 exo and LbCas12a, ExoIII (5 U/µl) triggered a substantial fluorescent signal promptly upon adding to FQ reporter (5 µM) (a total of 50 pmol), and most of the ssDNA substrate (over 90%) was cleaved in the first minute (Figure 1B), which suggested that the commercial ExoIII (5 U/µl) degraded over 2.7×1013 (45 pmol) phosphodiester bonds per minute in the reaction, significantly faster than 0.7 pmol phosphodiester bonds per minute of LbCas12a and that of other nucleases (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and calculations based on Figure 1B and 1C.

claim: At room temperature (22 °C), the fluorescence release initiated immediately when 0.5 µl ExoIII was mixed with FQ reporter (5 µM) under LED blue light.
source: Strikingly, we found even at room temperature (22 °C), the fluorescence release initiated immediately when 0.5 µl ExoIII was mixed with FQ reporter (5 µM) under LED blue light (Figure 1—video 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—video 1.

claim: T7 exo showed no significance with D-T7 exo.
source: In summary, T7 exo showed no significance with D-T7 exo; APE1 exhibited a significantly detectable fluorescence signal compared to its deactivated counterpart (D-APE1), albeit much weaker than that of ExoIII and LbCas12a (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: APE1 exhibited a significantly detectable fluorescence signal compared to its deactivated counterpart (D-APE1), albeit much weaker than that of ExoIII and LbCas12a.
source: In summary, T7 exo showed no significance with D-T7 exo; APE1 exhibited a significantly detectable fluorescence signal compared to its deactivated counterpart (D-APE1), albeit much weaker than that of ExoIII and LbCas12a (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: ExoIII (5 U/µl) digested over 90% of 5′ FAM T1-labeled FQ reporter (5 µM) in the first minute.
source: But fluorescence monitoring assays showed that ExoIII (5 U/µl) digested over 90% of 5′ FAM T1-labeled FQ reporter (5 µM) in the first minute (Figure 1E), indicating a speed of 2.7×1013 (45 pmol) phosphodiester bonds per minute (Figure 1F); APE1 and LbCas12a also exhibited a stronger fluorescence intensity compared to their deactivated counterparts (D-APE1 and D-LbCas12a) (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The evidence implied that ExoIII cleaved the FQ reporter not at 5′ end phosphodiesters.
source: The evidence implied that ExoIII cleaved the FQ reporter not at 5′ end phosphodiesters.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data on 5′ FAM T1-labeled FQ reporter.

claim: ExoIII cleaved over 90% of the base-labeled FQ reporter in 10 min.
source: Slower than the previous two FQ reporters, it cleaved over 90% of the base-labeled FQ reporter in 10 min (Figure 1H), demonstrating that the commercial ExoIII (5 U/µl) digested about 2.7×1012 (4.5 pmol) phosphodiester bonds or nucleotides of ssDNA in the FQ reporter (Figure 1I).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: The commercial ExoIII (5 U/µl) digested about 2.7×10^12 (4.5 pmol) phosphodiester bonds or nucleotides of ssDNA in the base-labeled FQ reporter.
source: Slower than the previous two FQ reporters, it cleaved over 90% of the base-labeled FQ reporter in 10 min (Figure 1H), demonstrating that the commercial ExoIII (5 U/µl) digested about 2.7×1012 (4.5 pmol) phosphodiester bonds or nucleotides of ssDNA in the FQ reporter (Figure 1I).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and calculations based on Figure 1H and 1I.

claim: The modifications on thymine may impede the binding and cleaving of the LbCas12a-crRNA complex on the ssDNA substrate, leading to less fluorescence generated.
source: Compared with the massive fluorescence induced by ExoIII, the modifications on thymine may impede the binding and cleaving of the LbCas12a-crRNA complex on the ssDNA substrate, leading to less fluorescence generated (Figure 1I).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: ExoIII might harbor a powerful ssDNase activity.
source: Combining all the results of three types of FQ reporters, we demonstrated ExoIII might harbor a powerful ssDNase activity.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data on three types of FQ reporters.

claim: The ssDNA was degraded by ExoIII and LbCas12a compared with the undigested product of APE1 and T7 exo.
source: After 40 min of incubation with ExoIII (5 U/µl) at 37 °C, the reaction mixture of three probes was separated by gel electrophoresis. The result indicated that the ssDNA was degraded by ExoIII and LbCas12a compared with the undigested product of APE1 and T7 exo (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and C.

claim: The reaction products gradually decreased in length as time prolonged, suggesting that ExoIII shortened Probe 1 into smaller fragments gradually and rapidly from 3′ to 5′ end.
source: The reaction products gradually decreased in length as time prolonged (Figure 2D), suggesting that ExoIII shortened Probe 1 into smaller fragments gradually and rapidly from 3′ to 5′ end.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D and inference from the data.

claim: The digesting rate of ExoIII on the ssDNA stood at 20~400 pmol nucleotides per minute in the 15 min.
source: The time course analysis on the digestion demonstrated the digesting rate of ExoIII on the ssDNA stood at 20~400 pmol nucleotides per minute in the 15 min (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and calculations shown in Figure 2E.

claim: ExoIII (5 U/µl) digested the ssDNA (5 µM) in the 3′→5′ direction with an estimated average speed of approximately 1.5×10^13 (25 pmol) phosphodiester bonds or nucleotides per minute.
source: The gradual and successive degradation on the three ssDNA substrates in the 40 min indicated that ExoIII (5 U/µl) digested the ssDNA (5 µM) in the 3′→5′ direction with an estimated average speed of approximately 1.5×1013 (25 pmol) phosphodiester bonds or nucleotides per minute, and the digestion rate varied with the encountered nucleotides of ssDNA substrate.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and calculations from time course analysis.

claim: The digestion rate of ExoIII varied with the encountered nucleotides of ssDNA substrate.
source: The gradual and successive degradation on the three ssDNA substrates in the 40 min indicated that ExoIII (5 U/µl) digested the ssDNA (5 µM) in the 3′→5′ direction with an estimated average speed of approximately 1.5×1013 (25 pmol) phosphodiester bonds or nucleotides per minute, and the digestion rate varied with the encountered nucleotides of ssDNA substrate.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data on three different ssDNA probes.

claim: ExoIII required 10 min to digest the 30-nt single-stranded DNA (ssDNA), whereas it could digest the same sequence on double-stranded DNA (dsDNA) within 1 min.
source: The result showed that ExoIII required 10 min to digest the 30-nt single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), whereas it could digest the same sequence on double-stranded DNA (dsDNA) within 1 min (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and 1B.

claim: ExoIII digested the dsDNA at a rate at least ten times faster than ssDNA.
source: This indicated that ExoIII digested the dsDNA at a rate at least ten times faster than ssDNA.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data comparing digestion rates on ssDNA and dsDNA.

claim: The ssDNase activity of ExoIII surpasses that of the conventional ssDNA-specific nuclease ExoI, suggesting a potential biological significance of ExoIII in bacteria related to ssDNA metabolism.
source: Even not as rapid as the dsDNA, the ssDNase activity of ExoIII surpasses that of the conventional ssDNA-specific nuclease ExoI (Shen et al., 2023), suggesting a potential biological significance of ExoIII in bacteria related to ssDNA metabolism.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data and citation to Shen et al., 2023.

claim: The structure of the αM helix of ExoIII deteriorated in APE1.
source: To investigate the massive disparity of ssDNase activity between the two highly similar homologs, ExoIII and APE1, we performed structure alignment and found the structure of the αM helix of ExoIII deteriorated in APE1 (Figure 2N).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 2N.

claim: The αM helix lies in the binding interface of ExoIII and substrate and might play a critical role in the digestion of ssDNA.
source: As αM lies in the binding interface of ExoIII and substrate (Mol et al., 1995), it might play a critical role in the digestion of ssDNA.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from structural analysis and citation to Mol et al., 1995.

claim: The degenerated ssDNA-cleavage activity of APE1 may evolve to minimize the risk of genomic instability in human.
source: The degenerated ssDNA-cleavage activity of APE1 may evolve to minimize the risk of genomic instability in human.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on inference from the observed differences between ExoIII and APE1.

claim: After being treated with ExoIII, Probe 1 was digested to three major products (P1P1, P1P2, P1P3) which respectively matched to an 8-nt, 7-nt and 16-nt ssDNA fragments of Probe 1.
source: After being treated with ExoIII, Probe 1 was digested to the three major products (Product 1 of Probe 1, termed as P1P1, Mass peak = 2914.9 Da; P1P2, Mass peak = 2601.5 Da; P1P3, Mass peak = 5395.5 Da) (Figure 3A), which respectively matched to an 8-nt (Theoretical mass = 2915.6 Da), 7-nt (Theoretical mass = 2602.4 Da) and 16-nt (Theoretical mass = 5397.2 Da) ssDNA fragments of Probe 1, and these undigested nucleatides accounted for ~15% of the input (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 3A and 3B.

claim: The undigested nucleotides of Probe 1 accounted for ~15% of the input.
source: After being treated with ExoIII, Probe 1 was digested to the three major products (Product 1 of Probe 1, termed as P1P1, Mass peak = 2914.9 Da; P1P2, Mass peak = 2601.5 Da; P1P3, Mass peak = 5395.5 Da) (Figure 3A), which respectively matched to an 8-nt (Theoretical mass = 2915.6 Da), 7-nt (Theoretical mass = 2602.4 Da) and 16-nt (Theoretical mass = 5397.2 Da) ssDNA fragments of Probe 1, and these undigested nucleatides accounted for ~15% of the input (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data and calculations shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Probe 2 was digested to two major products (P2P1, P2P2) which respectively matched to a 13-nt and 3-nt ssDNA fragments of Probe 2.
source: Probe 2 was digested to two major products (P2P1, Mass peak = 4639.6 Da; P2P2, Mass peak = 957.7 Da) (Figure 3C), which respectively matched to a 13-nt (Theoretical mass = 4641.6 Da) and 3-nt (Theoretical mass = 957.6 Da) ssDNA fragments of Probe 2, and these remaining oligos accounted for ~0.6% of the input (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 3C and 3D.

claim: The remaining oligos of Probe 2 accounted for ~0.6% of the input.
source: Probe 2 was digested to two major products (P2P1, Mass peak = 4639.6 Da; P2P2, Mass peak = 957.7 Da) (Figure 3C), which respectively matched to a 13-nt (Theoretical mass = 4641.6 Da) and 3-nt (Theoretical mass = 957.6 Da) ssDNA fragments of Probe 2, and these remaining oligos accounted for ~0.6% of the input (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data and calculations shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Probe 3 was digested into four products (P3P1, P3P2, P3P3, P3P4) respectively matched to an 8-nt, 9-nt, 7-nt and 6-nt fragments of Probe 3.
source: Probe 3 was digested into four products (P3P1, Mass peak = 2936.9; P3P2, Mass peak = 3240.9; P3P3, Mass peak = 2632.7; P3P4, Mass peak = 2328.7) (Figure 3E) respectively matched to an 8-nt (Theoretical mass = 2937.6 Da), 9-nt (Theoretical mass = 3241.8 Da), 7-nt (Theoretical mass = 2633.4 Da) and 6-nt (Theoretical mass = 2329.2 Da) fragments of Probe 3, and these leftover accounted for ~28% of the input (Figure 3F).
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 3E and 3F.

claim: The leftover of Probe 3 accounted for ~28% of the input.
source: Probe 3 was digested into four products (P3P1, Mass peak = 2936.9; P3P2, Mass peak = 3240.9; P3P3, Mass peak = 2632.7; P3P4, Mass peak = 2328.7) (Figure 3E) respectively matched to an 8-nt (Theoretical mass = 2937.6 Da), 9-nt (Theoretical mass = 3241.8 Da), 7-nt (Theoretical mass = 2633.4 Da) and 6-nt (Theoretical mass = 2329.2 Da) fragments of Probe 3, and these leftover accounted for ~28% of the input (Figure 3F).
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data and calculations shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The majority of ssDNA substrates (5 µM) were degraded into mononucleotides (~85% for Probe 1, ~99% for Probe 2 and ~72% for Probe 3) by ExoIII (5 U/µl).
source: According to the mass peak intensities of reaction products (Table 2), the majority of ssDNA substrates (5 µM) were degraded into mononucleotides (~85% for Probe 1,~99% for Probe 2 and ~72% for Probe 3) by ExoIII (5 U/µl).
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data and calculations based on Table 2.

claim: These undigested fragments (P1P1, P1P2, P2P1, P3P1, P3P2, P3P3, and P3P4) retained an intact 5′ end fluorophore and a free 3′-OH, which indicated the ExoIII catalyzed the cleavage of ssDNA at the 5′-side bond of phosphodiester.
source: Furthermore, we found these undigested fragments above (P1P1, P1P2, P2P1, P3P1, P3P2, P3P3, and P3P4) retained an intact 5′ end fluorophore and a free 3′-OH, which indicated the ExoIII catalyzed the cleavage of ssDNA at the 5′-side bond of phosphodiester.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from mass spectrometry data analysis.

claim: 17 ssDNA fragments (four fragments from Probe 1 and 13 fragments from Probe 2) were identified from the middle part of the ssDNA, implying ExoIII possessed an endonuclease activity on ssDNA.

claim: Four primary functional units for enzymatic actions of ExoIII are defined: capturing unit (R170), phosphate-stabilizing unit (Y109, K121, and N153), sugar ring-stacking unit (W212, F213, and D214) and phosphodiester-cleaving unit (D151).
source: According to the ExoIII-ssDNA structure and the previously reported functions of the key residues (Lee et al., 2022), four primary functional units for enzymatic actions of ExoIII are defined: capturing unit (R170, at 3′ side of the cleavage site and three nucleotides away from it), phosphate-stabilizing unit (Y109, K121, and N153, at 5′ side of cleavage site and three nucleotides away from it), sugar ring-stacking unit (W212, F213, and D214) and phosphodiester-cleaving unit (D151), all of which also represent four sequential steps in the digestion process (Figure 7B).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from structural analysis and citation to Lee et al., 2022, shown in Figure 7B.

evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The ssDNA substrate tends to be captured by the outer-layered unit 1, then stabilized by the inter-layered units 2 and 3, finally cleaved by unit 4 of ExoIII, producing short fragments of ssDNA (endonuclease activity).
source: Combining with the structure analysis and the digestion results of Figures 2 and 3, we proposed the enzymatic actions of ExoIII digestion on ssDNA: the ssDNA substrate tends to be captured by the outer-layered unit 1, then stabilized by the inter-layered units 2 and 3, finally cleaved by unit 4 of ExoIII, producing short fragments of ssDNA (endonuclease activity).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from structural analysis and experimental data from Figures 2 and 3.

claim: When the 3′ flap occurs, ExoIII recognize and remove the ssDNA flap by the ssDNase activity; then it continues to digest the ssDNA on dsDNA and create a gap; the resulting intermediate recruits the DNA polymerase to re-synthesize the complementary strand and fill the ssDNA gap; finally, the nick left is sealed by DNA ligase.
source: Based on our results and the gap creation ability of ExoIII previously reported (Yoo et al., 2021), we proposed the novel biological role of ExoIII in DNA repair: when the 3′ flap occurs, ExoIII recognize and remove the ssDNA flap by the ssDNase activity; then it continues to digest the ssDNA on dsDNA and create a gap; the resulting intermediate recruits the DNA polymerase to re-synthesize the complementary strand and fill the ssDNA gap; finally, the nick left is sealed by DNA ligase (Figure 8D).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data and citation to Yoo et al., 2021, shown in Figure 8D.
